knowledge_statements.title: Bounded-Circulation Feasibility
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Hoffman’s finite directed bounded-circulation criterion.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(D=(V,A)\) be a finite directed graph with real arc bounds \(\ell_a\le u_a\). A circulation \(x\) satisfying \(\ell_a\le x_a\le u_a\) for every \(a\in A\) exists if and only if, for every subset \(S\subseteq V\),
\[
\ell(\delta^-(S))\le u(\delta^+(S)).
\]
Here bounds are summed over the indicated cut arcs. Equivalently, no vertex set requires more lower-bounded inflow than its outgoing arcs can carry. The inequalities for \(S=\varnothing\) and \(S=V\) are vacuous.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A bounded circulation exists exactly when every vertex set’s mandatory incoming flow is at most its available outgoing capacity.
assumptions_latex: \(\ell_a,u_a\in\mathbb R\) and \(\ell_a\le u_a\) for every arc.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\exists x:\operatorname{div}_x=0,\ \ell\le x\le u\iff \ell(\delta^-(S))\le u(\delta^+(S))\ \forall S\subseteq V.\)

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Integral residual-labeling procedure for repairing violated lower or upper arc bounds while preserving flow conservation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: On a finite directed network with integral bounds \(\ell(x,y)\le c(x,y)\), start from an integral flow \(f\) satisfying conservation at every node. While an arc \((s,t)\) violates a bound, perform the prescribed residual-labeling search for a correcting cycle through \((s,t)\). If breakthrough occurs, augment around that cycle by the admissible labeled amount; conservation and all previously satisfied arc bounds remain valid, while \(f(s,t)\) moves at least one unit toward \([\ell(s,t),c(s,t)]\). Repeat. The procedure terminates finitely either with \(\ell(x,y)\le f(x,y)\le c(x,y)\) on every arc or with a nonbreakthrough cut which, after orienting its sides appropriately, satisfies \[c(X,\bar X)<\ell(\bar X,X),\] certifying infeasibility.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Starting from an integral conserved flow, residual labeling finds cycles that correct bound-violating arcs. Each successful correction preserves conservation and already satisfied bounds. Finitely many corrections yield a feasible circulation, or a failed search yields a cut proving that none exists.
assumptions_latex: \(f\text{ is initially integral and satisfies flow conservation at every node}\)
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\text{The procedure terminates finitely with either a feasible circulation or some }X\subseteq N\text{ such that }c(X,\bar X)<\ell(\bar X,X).\)

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Tests lower-bounded circulation feasibility through one auxiliary maximum-flow computation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given \((D,\ell,u)\), initialize \(x=\ell\), set residual capacities \(c_a=u_a-\ell_a\), and define \(b(v)=\ell(\delta^-(v))-\ell(\delta^+(v))\). Add a supersource \(p\) and supersink \(q\); add \((p,v)\) of capacity \(b(v)\) when \(b(v)>0\), and \((v,q)\) of capacity \(-b(v)\) when \(b(v)<0\). Compute a maximum \(p\)-\(q\) flow \(y\). Output \(x_a=\ell_a+y_a\) on original arcs if every arc leaving \(p\) is saturated; otherwise output infeasible.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Shift by lower bounds, connect imbalance vertices to a supersource or supersink, and test whether maximum flow saturates every required repair arc.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Input a vector \(x\in\mathbb R^A\) satisfying \(\ell\le x\le u\), not necessarily conservation. Define \(d(v)=x(\delta^+(v))-x(\delta^-(v))\) and form the residual network \(D_x\) with forward capacity \(u_a-x_a\) and reverse capacity \(x_a-\ell_a\) for every \(a\in A\). While some vertex \(v\) has \(d(v)>0\), find a residual path from a vertex \(w\) with \(d(w)<0\) to \(v\), augment by the minimum of the path bottleneck, \(d(v)\), and \(-d(w)\), and update \(d\). Output \(x\) when \(d(v)=0\) for every \(v\in V\); if no such required path exists, output the corresponding residual cut obstruction.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Use residual paths from negative-imbalance vertices to positive-imbalance vertices until conservation holds, or return a blocking residual cut.

knowledge_statements.title: Source-Sink Flow Polyhedra
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Capacitated single-commodity flows with one source and one sink.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(D=(V,A)\) be a finite directed graph, let \(s,t\in V\) be distinct, and let \(u\in\mathbb{R}_{+}^{A}\). With node-arc incidence matrix \(B\), whose arc columns have \(-1\) at the tail and \(+1\) at the head, the source-sink flow polyhedron is
\[P_{s,t}(u)=\{(f,v)\in\mathbb{R}^{A}\times\mathbb{R}_{+}: Bf=v(e_t-e_s),\ 0\leq f\leq u\}.\]
Thus every intermediate node has zero net imbalance, the source has net outflow \(v\), and the sink has net inflow \(v\). Its projection onto arc variables is obtained by eliminating \(v\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The polyhedron consists of capacity-feasible arc flows conserving flow at intermediate nodes and carrying a nonnegative common value from the designated source to the designated sink.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(P_{s,t}(u)=\{(f,v)\in\mathbb{R}^{A}\times\mathbb{R}_{+}:Bf=v(e_t-e_s),\ 0\leq f\leq u\}\).

notation.meaning: Node-arc incidence matrix with head entry +1 and tail entry -1.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Bounded Source-Sink Flows and Associated Cut Capacity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines bounded directed source-sink flows, their value and maximum-flow formulation, the integral-optimum consequence for integral bounds, and the associated directed cut capacity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let $G$ be a loopless digraph with distinct vertices $v,w$. A $v$-$w$ flow is a vector $x\in\mathbb{R}^{E(G)}$ satisfying $\sum_{e\in\delta_G^+(u)}x_e-\sum_{e\in\delta_G^-(u)}x_e=0$ for every $u\in V(G)\setminus\{v,w\}$. Given $l:E(G)\to\mathbb{R}\cup\{-\infty\}$ and $c:E(G)\to\mathbb{R}\cup\{+\infty\}$, the flow is feasible if $l(e)\le x_e\le c(e)$ for every $e$. Its value satisfies $z(x):=\sum_{e\in\delta_G^+(v)}x_e-\sum_{e\in\delta_G^-(v)}x_e=\sum_{e\in\delta_G^-(w)}x_e-\sum_{e\in\delta_G^+(w)}x_e$. The maximum $v$-$w$ flow problem maximizes $z(x)$ over feasible flows and is a linear program. If all finite lower and upper bounds are integral, then an integer-valued optimal flow exists whenever an optimal solution exists. A $v$-$w$ cutset is a set $S\subset V(G)$ with $v\in S$ and $w\notin S$, with capacity $C(S):=\sum_{e\in\delta_G^+(S)}c(e)-\sum_{e\in\delta_G^-(S)}l(e)$.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A bounded source-sink flow conserves flow at every vertex except the distinct source and sink and respects the lower and upper arc bounds. Its net outflow from the source equals its net inflow to the sink. Maximum flow is the linear program maximizing this value; integral bounds yield an integral optimum whenever an optimum exists. A source-sink cut contains the source but not the sink, and its capacity is the sum of outgoing upper bounds minus the sum of incoming lower bounds.
assumptions_latex: \text{For the integrality conclusion, every finite value of }l\text{ and }c\text{ is integral, and an optimal solution exists}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: z(x)=\operatorname{netout}_v(x)=\operatorname{netin}_w(x);\quad \max\{z(x):x\text{ is feasible}\}\text{ is an LP; integral finite bounds admit an integral optimum when an optimum exists; and }C(S)=\sum_{e\in\delta_G^+(S)}c(e)-\sum_{e\in\delta_G^-(S)}l(e).

knowledge_statements.title: Bounded Circulation Polyhedra
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Circulations with lower and upper bounds on every arc.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(D=(V,A)\) be a finite directed graph with node-arc incidence matrix \(B\), and let \(\ell,u\in\mathbb{R}^{A}\) satisfy \(\ell\leq u\). The bounded circulation polyhedron is
\[P_{\mathrm{circ}}(\ell,u)=\{f\in\mathbb{R}^{A}:Bf=0,\ \ell\leq f\leq u\}.\]
The equation \(Bf=0\) imposes flow conservation at every node, while the componentwise inequalities impose the prescribed arc bounds. The polyhedron may be empty; when it is nonempty and both bound vectors are integral, every vertex is integral because the defining network matrix is totally unimodular.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A bounded circulation obeys flow conservation at every node and lies between prescribed lower and upper arc bounds; integral bounds give integral vertices.
assumptions_latex: \(D=(V,A)\) is finite with node-arc incidence matrix \(B\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(P_{\mathrm{circ}}(\ell,u)=\{f:Bf=0,\ \ell\leq f\leq u\}\), with integral vertices when \(\ell,u\in\mathbb{Z}^{A}\).

knowledge_statements.title: Transshipment Polyhedra
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Capacitated network flows realizing a prescribed node-balance vector.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(D=(V,A)\) be a finite directed graph with node-arc incidence matrix \(B\). For a balance vector \(b\in\mathbb{R}^{V}\) satisfying \(\sum_{v\in V}b_v=0\), and bounds \(\ell,u\in\mathbb{R}^{A}\) with \(\ell\leq u\), the transshipment polyhedron is
\[P(b,\ell,u)=\{f\in\mathbb{R}^{A}:Bf=b,\ \ell\leq f\leq u\}.\]
Under the incidence convention used here, positive \(b_v\) denotes net inflow demand and negative \(b_v\) denotes net supply. If \(b,\ell,u\) are integral, every vertex of a nonempty polyhedron \(P(b,\ell,u)\) is integral.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A transshipment flow satisfies prescribed node supplies and demands together with arc bounds; integral data produce an integral polyhedron.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(P(b,\ell,u)=\{f:Bf=b,\ \ell\leq f\leq u\}\), and integral data imply integral vertices.

notation.meaning: Node-balance vector; positive entries represent net demand.

knowledge_statements.title: Flow-Side Optimization Model
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Linear-programming formulation of the maximum source-sink flow problem.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For a finite directed graph \(D=(V,A)\), distinct nodes \(s,t\), capacities \(u\in\mathbb{R}_{+}^{A}\), and incidence matrix \(B\), the maximum-flow problem has the linear-programming representation
\[\max\{v:(f,v)\in\mathbb{R}^{A}\times\mathbb{R},\ Bf=v(e_t-e_s),\ 0\leq f\leq u\}.\]
The scalar \(v\) is the net outflow from \(s\), equivalently the net inflow into \(t\). Feasibility enforces conservation at every node outside \(\{s,t\}\), and maximizing \(v\) selects a feasible source-sink flow of greatest value.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Maximum flow is a linear program maximizing the common source outflow and sink inflow subject to conservation and capacity constraints.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\max v\) subject to \(Bf=v(e_t-e_s)\) and \(0\leq f\leq u\).

knowledge_statements.title: Cut-Side Dual Model
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Potential-form linear dual of the maximum-flow program.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Under the maximum-flow assumptions, assign a potential \(p_v\) to each node and a nonnegative variable \(z_a\) to each arc. A cut-side dual model is
\[\min\left\{\sum_{a\in A}u_a z_a:p_s=0,\ p_t=1,\ z_a\geq p_{\operatorname{head}(a)}-p_{\operatorname{tail}(a)},\ z_a\geq0\right\}.\]
Its optimum equals the maximum-flow value. An optimal potential may be chosen as the indicator of a set \(V\setminus S\), where \(s\in S\) and \(t\notin S\); then \(z\) indicates arcs leaving \(S\), and the objective is the capacity \(u(\delta^{+}(S))\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The flow LP dual minimizes weighted potential increases; an optimal binary potential identifies an source-sink cut whose capacity equals maximum flow.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\max\{v:Bf=v(e_t-e_s),\ 0\leq f\leq u\}=\min_{s\in S,\ t\notin S}u(\delta^{+}(S))\).

notation.meaning: Node-potential vector normalized by source and sink values.
Nonnegative arc variables dominating potential increases.
Arcs directed from the set S to its complement.

knowledge_statements.title: Complementary Flow-Cut Certificates
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Primal-dual optimality certificate using a feasible flow and a saturated cut.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(f\) be a feasible source-sink flow of value \(v\), and let \(S\subseteq V\) satisfy \(s\in S\) and \(t\notin S\). The pair \((f,S)\) certifies simultaneous flow and cut optimality if
\[f_a=u_a\quad(a\in\delta^{+}(S)),\qquad f_a=0\quad(a\in\delta^{-}(S)).\]
Flow conservation then gives
\[v=f(\delta^{+}(S))-f(\delta^{-}(S))=u(\delta^{+}(S)).\]
Every feasible flow has value at most every source-sink cut capacity, so this equality is directly checkable and certifies that \(f\) is maximum and \(S\) is minimum.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A feasible flow and cut are jointly optimal when every forward cut arc is saturated and every reverse cut arc carries zero flow.
assumptions_latex: \(f\) is a feasible source-sink flow of value \(v\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(v=u(\delta^{+}(S))\), so \(f\) is maximum and \(S\) is a minimum cut.

notation.meaning: Sum of capacities over an arc set F.

knowledge_statements.title: Node-Arc Incidence Matrices
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Signed incidence representation of conservation in a finite loopless directed graph.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For a finite loopless directed graph \(D=(V,A)\), its node-arc incidence matrix is \(B\in\{-1,0,1\}^{V\times A}\) defined for an arc \(a=(i,j)\), where \(i\neq j\), by
\[B_{va}=\begin{cases}-1,&v=i,\\+1,&v=j,\\0,&v\notin\{i,j\}.\end{cases}\]
Consequently, for any arc vector \(f\in\mathbb{R}^{A}\), the coordinate \((Bf)_v\) equals total inflow to \(v\) minus total outflow from \(v\). Every column sums to zero, and if the underlying undirected graph has \(k\) connected components, then \(\operatorname{rank}(B)=|V|-k\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: In a finite loopless directed graph, an incidence column has minus one at an arc's tail and plus one at its distinct head, so matrix multiplication records node imbalance.
assumptions_latex: \(D=(V,A)\) is a finite loopless directed graph.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \((Bf)_v\) is net inflow at \(v\), and \(\operatorname{rank}(B)=|V|-k\).

notation.meaning: Number of connected components of the underlying undirected graph.

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: standard signed-incidence definition and rank formula for loopless directed graphs

knowledge_statements.title: Total-Unimodularity Route
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Integrality of network-flow polyhedra derived from total unimodularity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The node-arc incidence matrix \(B\) of every directed graph is totally unimodular: every square subdeterminant belongs to \(\{-1,0,1\}\). Appending unit rows and changing row signs preserves total unimodularity, so the constraint matrix formed from \(B\), \(-B\), \(I\), and \(-I\) is totally unimodular. Therefore, if \(b,\ell,u\) are integral, every vertex of
\[\{f\in\mathbb{R}^{A}:Bf=b,\ \ell\leq f\leq u\}\]
is integral whenever this polyhedron is nonempty. This supplies the total-unimodularity route to integrality for circulations, transshipments, and source-sink flows.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Directed incidence matrices are totally unimodular; hence network-flow polyhedra with integral balances and bounds have only integral vertices.
assumptions_latex: \(B\) is the node-arc incidence matrix of a finite directed graph.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\{f:Bf=b,\ \ell\leq f\leq u\}\) is an integral polyhedron when nonempty.

notation.meaning: Identity matrix indexed by the arcs.

knowledge_statements.title: Total-Dual-Integrality Route
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Network-polyhedron integrality obtained through integral optimal dual solutions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Write the bounded network system \(Bf=b\), \(\ell\leq f\leq u\) as inequalities using \(Bf\leq b\), \(-Bf\leq-b\), \(f\leq u\), and \(-f\leq-\ell\). This system is totally dual integral: for every integral objective \(c\in\mathbb{Z}^{A}\) whose primal maximum is finite, the linear-programming dual has an integral optimal multiplier vector. When \(b,\ell,u\) are integral, total dual integrality implies that the associated polyhedron is integral. Thus integral optimal flows and integral dual certificates can be selected for all bounded integral network-flow instances with finite optimum.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The bounded network-flow inequality system is totally dual integral, yielding integral primal vertices and integral optimal dual certificates for integral data.
assumptions_latex: \(B\) is a directed node-arc incidence matrix.
\(b,\ell,u\) and the optimized objective vector are integral.
The relevant primal optimum is finite.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The bounded network system is TDI, and integral right-hand sides yield an integral polyhedron.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Maximum-flow algorithm for networks with nonnegative integral capacities.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Initialize $f(e)=0$ for every $e\in E(G)$. While the residual graph $G_f$ contains an $s$-$t$ path $P$, set $\gamma=\min_{a\in E(P)}u_f(a)$ and augment $f$ along $P$ by $\gamma$. When no augmenting path remains, return $f$; for integral capacities the procedure terminates with a maximum $s$-$t$ flow.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Start with zero flow and repeatedly augment by the bottleneck residual capacity of any residual source-to-sink path. With integral capacities, the process terminates and returns a maximum flow.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \text{Upon termination, }f\text{ is a maximum }s\text{-}t\text{ flow.

knowledge_statements.title: Generic Augmenting-Path Method
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Ford-Fulkerson with an arbitrary residual source-sink path rule.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Input a finite directed network \(D=(V,A)\), distinct \(s,t\), and capacities \(u\in\mathbb{R}_{+}^{A}\). Initialize \(f=0\). Given feasible \(f\), form the residual network with forward residual capacity \(u_a-f_a\) and reverse residual capacity \(f_a\). If it contains an \(s\)-to-\(t\) path \(P\), set \(\Delta=\min_{e\in P}r_e\), increase \(f_a\) by \(\Delta\) on forward occurrences, decrease it by \(\Delta\) on reverse occurrences, and repeat. If no such path exists, output \(f\) and the set \(S\) of vertices reachable from \(s\); then \((f,S)\) is a maximum-flow/minimum-cut certificate.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Repeatedly augment along any residual source-sink path by its bottleneck capacity; when no path remains, return the maximum flow and reachable minimum cut.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: If the method stops, its output \(f\) is maximum and the residual reachable set \(S\) is a minimum cut.

notation.meaning: Residual capacity of residual arc e.
Bottleneck residual capacity along the chosen path.

knowledge_statements.title: Integral-Capacity Termination
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite termination of arbitrary Ford-Fulkerson augmentations for integer capacities.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let all arc capacities be nonnegative integers, initialize the Ford-Fulkerson method with the zero flow, and choose any residual source-sink path at each iteration. Every residual capacity and every augmentation amount \(\Delta\) remains integral; hence each augmentation increases the flow value by at least \(1\). If \(F^{*}\) denotes the maximum-flow value, the algorithm performs at most \(F^{*}\) augmentations and terminates with a maximum flow. The same conclusion holds from any integral feasible initial flow, with at most \(F^{*}-v_0\) augmentations when its initial value is \(v_0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: With integer capacities and an integral initial flow, every augmentation raises flow value by at least one, so arbitrary Ford-Fulkerson path choices terminate.
assumptions_latex: The initial feasible flow is integral.
Each iteration chooses a residual source-sink path when one exists.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The method terminates after at most \(F^{*}-v_0\) augmentations and returns a maximum flow.

notation.meaning: Value of the initial integral feasible flow.

knowledge_statements.title: Flow-Value-Dependent Complexity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Pseudopolynomial running-time bound for integral-capacity Ford-Fulkerson.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Assume integer capacities, the zero initial flow, adjacency-list storage, and a path search requiring \(O(|V|+|A|)\) time. Since every Ford-Fulkerson augmentation increases the flow value by at least \(1\), at most \(F^{*}\) augmentations occur. The total running time is therefore
\[O\bigl((|V|+|A|)F^{*}\bigr),\]
or \(O(|A|F^{*})\) when every relevant vertex is incident to an arc. This bound is pseudopolynomial: \(F^{*}\) can be exponentially large in the binary encoding length of the capacities, so it is not a polynomial bound in the input bit length.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Ford-Fulkerson with integer capacities takes at most the maximum-flow value many augmentations, giving pseudopolynomial time proportional to path-search cost times that value.
assumptions_latex: Capacities are nonnegative integers encoded in binary.
The algorithm starts from zero flow.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The running time is \(O((|V|+|A|)F^{*})\), which is pseudopolynomial in binary input size.

knowledge_statements.title: Irrational-Capacity Nontermination
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Failure of arbitrary Ford–Fulkerson path selection with nonnegative real capacities.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let a finite directed network have source \(s\), sink \(t\), and capacities \(u_e\in\mathbb{R}_{\ge 0}\). Ford–Fulkerson repeatedly selects any residual \(s\)-\(t\) path and augments by its bottleneck residual capacity. If all capacities are integral, every positive augmentation increases the flow value by at least one; this termination mechanism disappears for irrational capacities. There exist networks with irrational capacities and admissible infinite path-selection sequences whose augmentation amounts tend to zero, so the generated feasible flows never attain a maximum flow and their values may converge to a value strictly below the maximum-flow value.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Irrational capacities permit infinite Ford–Fulkerson augmentation sequences with vanishing increments, potentially converging below the maximum-flow value.
assumptions_latex: Augmenting paths may be selected arbitrarily.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\text{Ford--Fulkerson need not terminate, and }\lim_k |f_k|<|f^*|\text{ can occur.}\)

knowledge_statements.title: Shortest Augmenting-Path Methods
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Unit-length shortest residual paths, including the Edmonds–Karp selection rule.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Input a feasible flow \(f\) in a finite capacitated network with source \(s\) and sink \(t\). At iteration \(k\), assign length one to every arc of the residual graph \(G_{f_k}\), find an \(s\)-\(t\) path \(P_k\) having the fewest arcs, and set \(\delta_k=\min_{e\in P_k}u_{f_k}(e)\). Augment \(f_k\) by \(\delta_k\) along \(P_k\), including the usual cancellation on reverse residual arcs. Stop and output \(f_k\) when no residual \(s\)-\(t\) path exists; the output is then a maximum flow.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Repeatedly augment along a residual path with the fewest arcs; absence of such a path certifies maximum flow.
assumptions_latex: \(G=(V,E)\) is finite and all capacities are nonnegative.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(P_k\in\arg\min_P |P|\), and termination returns a maximum flow.

knowledge_statements.title: Maximum-Capacity Augmenting-Path Methods
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Widest-path selection by maximum residual bottleneck capacity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given a feasible flow \(f_k\), define the width of a residual \(s\)-\(t\) path \(P\) by \(b_{f_k}(P)=\min_{e\in P}u_{f_k}(e)\). Select a widest augmenting path \(P_k\in\arg\max_P b_{f_k}(P)\), augment by \(b_{f_k}(P_k)\), and update forward and reverse residual capacities. A widest path may be found by labeling \(s\) with \(+\infty\), repeatedly giving each vertex the largest achievable bottleneck label, and stopping when \(t\) is finalized. If no residual \(s\)-\(t\) path exists, output the current flow as maximum.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: At every iteration, augment along a residual path whose bottleneck capacity is largest among all residual source–sink paths.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(b_{f_k}(P_k)=\max_P\min_{e\in P}u_{f_k}(e)\).

notation.meaning: widest residual path at iteration k

knowledge_statements.title: Price-Based Path Construction
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Construction of a residual path from exact distance-price labels.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Input a residual graph \(G_f\), source \(s\), sink \(t\), and labels \(p(v)\) equal to the minimum number of residual arcs from \(v\) to \(t\), with \(p(v)=+\infty\) when \(t\) is unreachable. If \(p(s)=+\infty\), report that no augmenting path exists. Otherwise initialize \(v=s\) and an empty path. While \(v\ne t\), choose a residual arc \((v,w)\) satisfying \(p(v)=p(w)+1\), append it, and replace \(v\) by \(w\). Output the resulting simple \(s\)-\(t\) path and augment by its residual bottleneck.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Follow residual arcs whose price labels decrease by one; exact distance labels guarantee arrival at the sink along a shortest path.
assumptions_latex: \(p(v)\) is the residual arc distance from \(v\) to \(t\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(p(s)<+\infty\) implies construction of an augmenting path \(P\) with \(|P|=p(s)\).

notation.meaning: distance-price label from v to the sink

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Maintains a simple forward path and integer node prices while seeking an s-to-t path.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let $(\mathcal N,\mathcal A)$ be a directed graph with $N=|\mathcal N|$ and specified nodes $s,t$. Initialize $P=(s)$ and integer prices satisfying $p_i\le p_j+1$ for every $(i,j)\in\mathcal A$, $p_s<N$, and $p_t=0$. Maintain a simple path $P=(s,n_1,\ldots,n_k)$ satisfying $p_i\ge p_j$ on every path arc. At the endpoint $n_k$, if $N(n_k)=\varnothing$, set $p_{n_k}=N$ and proceed to contraction. Otherwise select $\operatorname{succ}(n_k)\in\arg\min_{j\in N(n_k)}p_j$ and set $p_{n_k}=p_{\operatorname{succ}(n_k)}+1$. Extend to this successor if $n_k=s$ or $p_{\operatorname{pred}(n_k)}>p_{\operatorname{succ}(n_k)}$; otherwise contract by deleting the last path arc. Stop with the maintained path when an extension reaches $t$, or stop with the no-path outcome when $P=(s)$ and $p_s\ge N$.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Starting with the singleton path at s, repeatedly relabel its endpoint from the minimum-price outgoing neighbor. Extend when the price test permits and otherwise delete the last path arc. Stop upon reaching t or when the singleton source path has source price at least the number of nodes.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \text{The stated stopping outcomes are an }s\text{-}t\text{ forward path upon reaching }t\text{ and the no-path report when }P=(s),\ p_s\ge N.

knowledge_statements.title: Price-Label Maintenance
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Bellman consistency conditions for residual distance-price labels.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a residual graph \(G_f=(V,E_f)\) and sink \(t\), a distance-price labeling is a map \(p:V\to\mathbb{Z}_{\ge0}\cup\{+\infty\}\) satisfying \(p(t)=0\) and, for every \(v\ne t\), \[p(v)=\min_{(v,w)\in E_f}\bigl(1+p(w)\bigr),\] where the minimum over an empty set is \(+\infty\). After an augmentation changes \(E_f\), labels are maintained by applying these Bellman updates until every vertex again satisfies the displayed equality. A finite label then equals the minimum number of residual arcs from that vertex to \(t\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Price labels satisfy residual Bellman equations and are updated after augmentation until they again equal distances to the sink.
assumptions_latex: Every residual arc has unit length.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(p(v)=\operatorname{dist}_{G_f}(v,t)\) for every \(v\in V\).

notation.meaning: price or distance label of vertex v

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Residual-distance properties of successive shortest augmenting paths in Edmonds–Karp.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let $f_1,f_2,\ldots$ be flows such that $f_{i+1}$ results from $f_i$ by augmentation along a shortest $f_i$-augmenting path $P_i$. Then $|E(P_k)|\leq |E(P_{k+1})|$ for every $k$. Moreover, for every $k<l$ such that $P_k\cup P_l$ contains a pair of reverse edges, $|E(P_k)|+2\leq |E(P_l)|$.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For successive augmentations along shortest augmenting paths, path lengths never decrease. If an earlier and a later path together contain a pair of reverse edges, the later path is at least two edges longer.
assumptions_latex: f_{i+1}\text{ results from }f_i\text{ by augmentation along }P_i.
P_i\text{ is a shortest }f_i\text{-augmenting path for every }i.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \forall k,\ |E(P_k)|\leq |E(P_{k+1})|,\qquad \forall k<l,\ \bigl(P_k\cup P_l\text{ contains a pair of reverse edges}\bigr)\Rightarrow |E(P_k)|+2\leq |E(P_l)|.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Shortest-augmenting-path algorithm for maximum flow.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given a capacitated network $(G,u,s,t)$, initialize $f(e):=0$ for every $e\in E(G)$. Repeatedly choose a shortest $f$-augmenting path $P$, set $\gamma:=\min_{e\in E(P)}u_f(e)$, and augment $f$ along $P$ by $\gamma$. Stop when no $f$-augmenting path exists; the resulting $f$ is a maximum $s$-$t$ flow.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Initialize the flow to zero. Repeatedly augment by the minimum residual capacity along a shortest augmenting path. When no augmenting path remains, return the resulting maximum source-to-sink flow.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: f\text{ is a maximum }s\text{-}t\text{ flow upon termination.}

knowledge_statements.title: Breadth-First Residual Search
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Breadth-first implementation of Edmonds–Karp path selection.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given the residual graph \(G_f\), initialize a first-in-first-out queue with \(s\), set \(d(s)=0\), and leave all other vertices undiscovered. Repeatedly remove the queue head \(v\); for each residual arc \((v,w)\) with \(w\) undiscovered, set \(d(w)=d(v)+1\), record predecessor \(v\), and enqueue \(w\). If \(t\) is discovered, predecessor pointers recover an \(s\)-\(t\) residual path with the fewest arcs. If the queue empties without discovering \(t\), no augmenting path exists and the current feasible flow is maximum.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Breadth-first search finds a minimum-arc residual augmenting path or certifies that none exists.
assumptions_latex: All residual arcs are assigned unit length.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(d(t)=\operatorname{dist}_{G_f}(s,t)\), or \(t\) is unreachable from \(s\).

notation.meaning: residual graph of the current flow

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Monotonicity and critical-edge progress in Edmonds–Karp.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f_k\) be the flow before the \(k\)-th Edmonds–Karp augmentation, and let \(d_k(v)\) be the minimum number of arcs in a residual path from \(s\) to \(v\), with value \(+\infty\) if none exists. knowledge_statements.title: Strongly Polynomial Complexity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Edmonds–Karp bound independent of capacity magnitudes.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a directed network with \(n=|V|\) vertices and \(m=|E|\) original arcs, Edmonds–Karp performs \(O(nm)\) augmentations. A breadth-first residual search and the corresponding augmentation require \(O(m)\) arithmetic operations under an adjacency-list representation. Consequently, the algorithm computes a maximum flow in \(O(nm^2)\) arithmetic operations and \(O(n+m)\) working storage. The operation count depends only polynomially on \(n\) and \(m\), not on capacity values or their encoding lengths, so this is a strongly polynomial bound in the arithmetic model.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Edmonds–Karp uses at most order nm augmentations and order nm² arithmetic operations, independently of capacity magnitudes.
assumptions_latex: Residual breadth-first search uses adjacency lists.
Exact arithmetic operations have unit cost.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(N_{\mathrm{aug}}=O(nm)\) and \(T(n,m)=O(nm^2)\).

knowledge_statements.title: Residual-Capacity Thresholds
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Threshold residual graph used by capacity-scaling augmentation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a feasible flow \(f\) and threshold \(\Delta>0\), the \(\Delta\)-residual graph is \(G_f(\Delta)=(V,E_f(\Delta))\), where \[E_f(\Delta)=\{e\in E_f:u_f(e)\ge\Delta\}.\] A \(\Delta\)-augmenting path is an \(s\)-\(t\) path in \(G_f(\Delta)\). Its residual bottleneck is at least \(\Delta\), so augmentation along it increases the flow value by at least \(\Delta\). For integral capacities bounded by \(U\), capacity scaling starts with \(\Delta=2^{\lfloor\log_2 U\rfloor}\) and subsequently halves \(\Delta\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A threshold residual graph retains exactly arcs with residual capacity at least Δ; every path in it supports an augmentation of at least Δ.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(P\subseteq G_f(\Delta)\) implies \(\min_{e\in P}u_f(e)\ge\Delta\).

knowledge_statements.title: Scaling-Phase Structure
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Phase organization of binary capacity-scaling Ford–Fulkerson.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Assume integral capacities and let \(U=\max_e u_e\). Initialize \(f=0\) and \(\Delta=2^{\lfloor\log_2 U\rfloor}\). During a \(\Delta\)-phase, repeatedly find an \(s\)-\(t\) path in \(G_f(\Delta)\) and augment along it by its full residual bottleneck. When no such path remains, replace \(\Delta\) by \(\Delta/2\). Continue through the \(\Delta=1\) phase and then output \(f\). At the end of every phase, no residual \(s\)-\(t\) path has all arc capacities at least the current threshold; after the final phase, no residual augmenting path exists.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Capacity scaling exhausts augmenting paths above a threshold, halves the threshold, and finishes after the unit-capacity phase.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: After the \(\Delta=1\) phase, \(f\) is a maximum flow.

knowledge_statements.title: Weakly Polynomial Complexity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Binary capacity-scaling bound with logarithmic dependence on maximum capacity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(n=|V|\), \(m=|E|\), and let integral capacities satisfy \(0\le u_e\le U\). Binary capacity scaling has at most \(1+\lfloor\log_2 U\rfloor\) phases. With full-bottleneck augmentation, each phase performs \(O(m)\) augmentations, and each residual path search plus update costs \(O(m)\) time using graph search and adjacency lists. Thus a maximum flow is obtained in \(O(m^2\log U)\) time. The dependence on \(\log U\), an input encoding parameter, makes this bound weakly polynomial rather than strongly polynomial.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Binary capacity scaling computes maximum flow in order m² log U time, so its bound depends on numerical capacity encoding.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(N_{\mathrm{aug}}=O(m\log U)\) and \(T=O(m^2\log U)\).

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Specifies the level-graph and blocking-flow phase procedure, including augmentation through forward and reverse residual arcs.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Initialize $f(e)=0$ for all $e\in E(G)$. Repeatedly construct $G_f^L$ and find a blocking $s$-$t$ flow $f'$ in $(G_f^L,u_f)$. If $f'=0$, stop and return $f$. knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Start with zero flow. In each phase construct the residual level graph, find a blocking flow in it, and augment along its forward and reverse residual arcs. Stop when the blocking flow is zero; the specified output is a maximum flow.

knowledge_statements.title: Level Networks
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Dinic level graph formed from residual shortest-path distances.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G_f=(V,E_f)\) be the residual graph of a feasible flow, and define \(d(v)=\operatorname{dist}_{G_f}(s,v)\), taking \(d(v)=+\infty\) when \(v\) is unreachable. The level network is the directed graph \(L_f=(V_f,E_f^L)\), where \(V_f=\{v:d(v)<+\infty\}\) and \[E_f^L=\{(v,w)\in E_f:d(w)=d(v)+1\}.\] Every directed path in \(L_f\) strictly increases the level at each arc; consequently, \(L_f\) is acyclic, and every \(s\)-\(t\) path in it has exactly \(d(t)\) arcs and is shortest in \(G_f\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A Dinic level network keeps residual arcs advancing exactly one BFS level; it is acyclic and contains precisely shortest source–sink paths.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \((v,w)\in E_f^L\Rightarrow d(w)=d(v)+1\), so \(L_f\) is acyclic.

notation.meaning: level network of the current flow

knowledge_statements.title: Blocking-Flow Subproblems
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Blocking flow in Dinic's residual level network.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f\) be a feasible \(s\)-\(t\) flow, let \(d_f(v)\) be the residual distance from \(s\), and let \(L_f\) contain precisely the residual arcs \((u,v)\) satisfying \(d_f(v)=d_f(u)+1\). A feasible \(s\)-\(t\) flow \(g\) in \(L_f\), bounded by the level-arc capacities \(c_f\), is blocking if every directed \(s\)-\(t\) path in \(L_f\) contains an arc \(e\) with \(g(e)=c_f(e)\). Equivalently, the subgraph of \(L_f\) containing precisely the level arcs \(e\) with \(g(e)<c_f(e)\) has no directed \(s\)-\(t\) path.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A blocking flow respects the level-network capacities and saturates at least one arc on every source-to-sink path; equivalently, its unsaturated forward level arcs contain no source-to-sink path.
assumptions_latex: \(G=(V,E)\) is a finite directed capacitated network with source \(s\) and sink \(t\).
\(t\) is reachable from \(s\) in the residual graph of \(f\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(g\text{ is blocking}\iff t\text{ is unreachable from }s\text{ using unsaturated forward arcs of }L_f.\)

knowledge_statements.title: Phasewise Distance Growth
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Strict residual-distance growth between completed Dinic phases.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f\) be the flow at the beginning of a Dinic phase, let \(d_f(t)<\infty\), and augment \(f\) by a blocking flow in its level network to obtain \(f'\). If \(t\) remains reachable from \(s\) in the residual graph of \(f'\), then \(d_{f'}(t)>d_f(t)\). If \(t\) is unreachable, the algorithm terminates with a maximum flow. Thus no two completed nonterminal phases have the same source-to-sink residual distance.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: After each blocking-flow phase, the residual source-to-sink distance strictly increases unless the sink becomes unreachable and the algorithm terminates.
assumptions_latex: \(f'\) is obtained from \(f\) by augmenting a blocking flow in the level network of \(f\).

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: In a finite network with \(n=|V|\), every nonterminal Dinic phase strictly increases the integral residual distance from \(s\) to \(t\). knowledge_statements.title: Aggregate Running-Time Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Classical Dinic bounds under adjacency-list unit-cost arithmetic.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(n=|V|\) and \(m=|E|\). With adjacency lists, breadth-first level construction costs \(O(m)\), and a current-arc blocking-flow computation costs \(O(nm)\); together with fewer than \(n\) phases this gives \(O(n^2m)\) time in general. Refined phase analyses give \(O(m\sqrt n)\) on unit networks and \(O\!\left(m\min\{n^{2/3},\sqrt m\}\right)\) on directed unit-capacity networks.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Classical Dinic runs in quadratic-vertex times edge complexity generally, with sharper bounds for unit and unit-capacity networks.
assumptions_latex: Graph traversal and capacity arithmetic take unit time.
The stated special-regime bounds use their standard structural definitions.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(T_{\mathrm{general}}=O(n^2m)\), \(T_{\mathrm{unit}}=O(m\sqrt n)\), and \(T_{\mathrm{unit\text{-}cap}}=O\!\left(m\min\{n^{2/3},\sqrt m\}\right)\).

knowledge_statements.title: Current-Arc Implementation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Pointer-based depth-first construction of one blocking flow.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For each vertex \(v\) of the acyclic level network, initialize a pointer \(p(v)\) to its first outgoing arc. Perform depth-first pushes from \(s\), using only the arc at \(p(v)\). Advance \(p(v)\) whenever that arc is saturated or cannot reach \(t\), and never move a pointer backward during the phase. Retreat from \(v\) after all its outgoing arcs are exhausted. Stop when no further positive push can leave \(s\); the accumulated augmentation is a blocking flow. Each pointer advances at most the outdegree of its vertex.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Persistent outgoing-arc pointers prevent rescanning rejected arcs while depth-first searches construct a blocking flow.
assumptions_latex: The input is a finite acyclic level network with nonnegative residual capacities.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\sum_{v\in V}\#\operatorname{advance}(p(v))\le |E|\), and the returned flow is blocking.

notation.meaning: current outgoing-arc pointer of vertex v

knowledge_statements.title: Karzanov Blocking Preflows
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Preflow-based blocking computation on an acyclic level network.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Initialize the zero preflow \(x\) on the level network. Repeatedly push residual capacity from an active internal vertex along outgoing level arcs while preserving \(0\le x(e)\le c_f(e)\). If an active vertex cannot send its excess forward, return that excess toward \(s\) along level arcs currently carrying positive flow and remove the exhausted vertex from further consideration. Continue until no internal vertex has excess. The resulting conserved \(s\)-\(t\) flow is blocking because every surviving level path has acquired a saturated or deleted arc.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Karzanov's routine builds a blocking flow through temporary vertex excesses, forward pushes, and removal of vertices that cannot transmit excess.
assumptions_latex: The input is a finite acyclic residual level network.
Capacities are nonnegative and pushes do not exceed residual capacity.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x\) terminates as a feasible blocking \(s\)-\(t\) flow in the level network.

knowledge_statements.title: Fujishige Blocking-Flow Variant
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Fujishige's blocking-flow routine; operational variant requires source confirmation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given an acyclic level network, initialize \(g=0\). Maintain a subnetwork of unsaturated arcs that can lie on an \(s\)-\(t\) path. Select such a path \(P\), augment by \(\delta=\min_{e\in P}(c_f(e)-g(e))\), delete newly saturated arcs, and recursively discard vertices that can no longer reach \(t\) or be reached from \(s\). Stop when \(t\) is unreachable. The accumulated feasible flow \(g\) is blocking.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The variant augments within a pruned level network until every source-to-sink path has a saturated arc.
assumptions_latex: The input is a finite acyclic level network with nonnegative residual capacities.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(g\) is feasible and every directed \(s\)-\(t\) path contains an arc \(e\) satisfying \(g(e)=c_f(e)\).

knowledge_statements.title: Dynamic-Tree Blocking Flows
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Link-cut-tree acceleration of path operations within a level network.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Represent the current forest of admissible level arcs by dynamic trees. A root path stores residual capacities and supports a minimum-capacity query, a uniform path decrement, linking an admissible arc, and cutting saturated arcs. To augment, link a current \(s\)-to-\(t\) admissible path, subtract its bottleneck from the path, and cut every arc attaining zero residual capacity; discard vertices with no admissible continuation. With amortized \(O(\log |V|)\) dynamic-tree operations and only \(O(|E|)\) links and cuts, one blocking flow is computed in \(O(|E|\log |V|)\) time.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Dynamic trees batch bottleneck queries and path updates, reducing one blocking-flow computation to near-linear time.
assumptions_latex: Dynamic-tree path operations take amortized \(O(\log |V|)\) time.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(T_{\mathrm{blocking}}=O(|E|\log |V|)\).

notation.meaning: time to compute one blocking flow
current residual capacity stored on arc e

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: No citation supports the particular dynamic-tree operations, the asserted O(|E|) operation count, or the resulting O(|E| log |V|) per-blocking-flow bound.

knowledge_statements.title: Blocking-Flow Scaling Hybrids
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Integral capacity scaling combined with layered blocking phases.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For integral capacities, start with zero flow and let \(\Delta\) be the largest power of two not exceeding \(U=\max_e c(e)\). At scale \(\Delta\), retain residual arcs with capacity at least \(\Delta\); repeatedly construct their level network and augment a blocking flow until \(t\) is unreachable in that thresholded residual graph. Then replace \(\Delta\) by \(\Delta/2\). After completing scale \(\Delta=1\), output the flow. Since every positive residual capacity is then at least one, termination implies that no residual \(s\)-\(t\) path exists.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The hybrid exhausts blocking flows on successively finer residual-capacity thresholds and returns a maximum integral flow after scale one.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(t\) is unreachable in the final residual graph, so the output is a maximum \(s\)-\(t\) flow.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The threshold-scaling construction is plausible, but no source identifies it as the intended blocking-flow scaling hybrid or supports its exact update and termination formulation.

knowledge_statements.title: Unit-Capacity Networks
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Directed maximum-flow networks whose arcs all have unit capacity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A directed \(s\)-\(t\) network \(G=(V,E,c)\) is unit-capacity if \(c(e)=1\) for every arc \(e\in E\). For an integral feasible flow \(f\), each original arc \(e\) carries \(f(e)\in\{0,1\}\). The forward and reverse residual copies associated with \(e\) have capacities \(1-f(e)\) and \(f(e)\), respectively, and hence each has capacity in \(\{0,1\}\). If the original network has parallel or antiparallel arcs, their residual copies are retained as distinct arcs.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A unit-capacity network gives every original directed arc capacity one. Under an integral flow, each original arc carries zero or one, and its separately represented forward and reverse residual copies have binary capacities.
assumptions_latex: \(G\) is a finite directed network with distinguished vertices \(s\) and \(t\).
Residual arcs associated with distinct original arcs are represented separately.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(G\text{ is unit-capacity}\iff (\forall e\in E)\,c(e)=1.\)

notation.meaning: integral flow on original arc e

knowledge_statements.title: Unit Networks

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A directed unit-capacity \(s\)-\(t\) network is a unit network if every internal vertex \(v\in V\setminus\{s,t\}\) satisfies at least one of the following: \(v\) has exactly one incoming arc, or \(v\) has exactly one outgoing arc. knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \((\forall v\in V\setminus\{s,t\})\,[\deg^-(v)=1\ \lor\ \deg^+(v)=1]\) and \((\forall e\in E)\,c(e)=1\).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Recovery of a maximum flow from the terminal preflow
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Second-phase feasibility construction and the stated single-phase alternative for preflow-push.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Suppose the first phase terminates with a saturated minimum cut $[\mathcal N^+,\mathcal N^-]$ such that $1\in\mathcal N^+$, $N\in\mathcal N^-$, $g_i\ge0$ for $i\in\mathcal N^+\setminus\{1\}$, and $g_i=0$ for $i\in\mathcal N^-\setminus\{N\}$. Delete the nodes in $\mathcal N^-$ and all their incident arcs. For each $i\in\mathcal N^+\setminus\{1\}$ for which
\[\sum_{j\in\mathcal N^-:(i,j)\in\mathcal A}c_{ij}>0,\]
add or reset an arc $(i,1)$ with
\[x_{i1}=c_{i1}=\sum_{j\in\mathcal N^-:(i,j)\in\mathcal A}c_{ij}.\]
Find a capacity-feasible flow $\bar x$ having zero surplus at every node of the resulting graph, and define
\[x^*_{ij}=\begin{cases}\bar x_{ij},&i,j\notin\mathcal N^-,\\x_{ij},&\text{otherwise}.\end{cases}\]
Then $x^*$ conserves flow at every nonterminal node, saturates the same minimum cut, and is a maximum flow. The second phase satisfies the same running-time bounds as the first, so the combined algorithm does also. A single-phase variant that permits iterations at every $i\ne N$ with $g_i>0$, including when $p_i\ge N$, likewise terminates within those bounds and returns a maximum flow.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Delete the sink side of the terminal minimum cut, add return arcs from appropriate source-side nodes to the source, and solve a zero-surplus feasibility problem to return accumulated excess. Combining that solution with the unchanged sink-side and cut flows gives a conserved maximum flow. The recovery phase has the first phase's running-time bounds. Processing every positive-surplus nonsink node also gives the stated single-phase variant.
assumptions_latex: [\mathcal N^+,\mathcal N^-]\text{ is the saturated minimum cut returned by the first phase}
g_i\ge0\ \forall i\in\mathcal N^+\setminus\{1\},\quad g_i=0\ \forall i\in\mathcal N^-\setminus\{N\}
\bar x\text{ is capacity-feasible and has zero surplus in the constructed auxiliary graph}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: x^*\text{ is a maximum flow, and the stated two-phase and single-phase implementations retain the preflow-push termination and running-time bounds.}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Termination, minimum-cut certificate, and complexity of preflow-push
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Correctness and selection-dependent running-time guarantees for the stated price-based preflow-push algorithm.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The preflow-push algorithm terminates. Upon termination, there is a saturated cut $[\mathcal N^+,\mathcal N^-]$ satisfying
\[1\in\mathcal N^+,\qquad N\in\mathcal N^-,\]
\[g_i\ge0\quad\forall i\in\mathcal N^+\setminus\{1\},\qquad g_i=0\quad\forall i\in\mathcal N^-\setminus\{N\}.\]
This saturated cut is a minimum cut. With arbitrary active-node selection the running time is $O(N^2A)$, and with FIFO active-node selection it is $O(N^3)$.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The algorithm terminates with a saturated minimum source–sink cut. Non-source nodes on the source side have nonnegative surplus, and nonsink nodes on the sink side have zero surplus. Arbitrary active-node selection takes O(N²A) time; FIFO selection takes O(N³).
assumptions_latex: \text{The stated preflow-push algorithm is run on a network with }N\text{ nodes and }A\text{ arcs}
\text{The algorithm maintains its stated flow–price and surplus invariants}

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a preflow \(x\), the excess of a vertex \(i\in N\) is \[e(i)=\sum_{j:(j,i)\in A}x_{ji}-\sum_{j:(i,j)\in A}x_{ij}.\] Thus \(e(i)\ge 0\) for every \(i\in N\setminus\{s,t\}\). knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f\) be a feasible flow whose residual graph \(G_f\) has no directed \(s\)-\(t\) path. Define \[S=\{v\in V:s\leadsto v\text{ in }G_f\}.\] Then \(s\in S\) and \(t\notin S\). Every original arc leaving \(S\) is saturated, while every original arc entering \(S\) carries zero flow; otherwise the corresponding residual arc would enlarge \(S\). Hence the flow value equals the capacity of the cut \(\delta^+(S)\). By weak flow-cut inequality, \(f\) is maximum and \(S\) is a minimum cut.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: If the residual graph has no source-to-sink path, the source-reachable vertices define a minimum cut.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Initialize a queue \(Q\) with all active vertices in any fixed order. Remove the front vertex \(u\), discharge \(u\) by admissible pushes and relabels until \(e_f(u)=0\), and append to the rear every vertex that becomes active and is not already queued. If \(u\) later becomes active again, append it in the same way. Continue until \(Q\) is empty. An empty queue implies no active intermediate vertex, so the resulting flow is maximum.

knowledge_statements.title: Gap Relabeling
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Gap heuristic for a valid distance labeling in a push-relabel maximum-flow algorithm.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G_f\) be the residual graph, let \(n=|V|\), and let \(h:V\to\{0,\ldots,2n-1\}\) be valid: \(h(t)=0\) and \(h(u)\le h(v)+1\) for every residual arc \((u,v)\). knowledge_statements.title: Excess Scaling
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Excess-threshold scheduling for push-relabel maximum flow.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given a preflow with excess \(e(v)\), initialize \(\Delta\) to a power of two at least \(\max_{v\ne s,t}e(v)\). During a \(\Delta\)-phase, select only vertices satisfying \(e(v)\ge\Delta\), perform admissible pushes and valid relabels, and avoid creating excess exceeding the phase's prescribed upper threshold. When no such active vertex remains, set \(\Delta\leftarrow\Delta/2\). Stop when \(\Delta<1\) for integral capacities, or when all intermediate excesses vanish. The resulting preflow is then a maximum flow under the usual push-relabel termination invariant.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Process vertices by decreasing powers-of-two excess thresholds; after the final phase, no intermediate vertex has excess and the preflow is a maximum flow.
assumptions_latex: Capacities and the initial preflow are integral.
Pushes use residual capacity and admissible arcs.
Relabel operations preserve a valid distance labeling.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: At termination, \(e(v)=0\) for every \(v\in V\setminus\{s,t\}\), and the resulting flow is maximum.

knowledge_statements.title: Dynamic-Tree Push-Relabel
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Push-relabel implementation that batches admissible pushes along represented residual paths.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Maintain the admissible residual arcs as a forest represented by dynamic trees, with each represented edge storing its residual capacity. For an active vertex \(v\), link admissible arcs to form a directed represented path toward a lower-label root, and push \(\delta=\min\{e(v),\min_{a\in P}r(a)\}\) simultaneously along the path \(P\). Update path residual capacities lazily; cut every edge that becomes saturated. If no admissible outgoing residual arc exists, relabel the vertex by the usual minimum-neighbor rule. Terminate when no intermediate vertex is active, and output the represented preflow as a maximum flow.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Dynamic trees batch pushes along admissible residual paths, supporting path bottlenecks and capacity updates while preserving ordinary push-relabel invariants.

Each linked arc is residual and admissible.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Termination yields a feasible maximum \(s\)-\(t\) flow.

knowledge_statements.title: Potential-Function Analysis
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Amortized accounting of nonsaturating pushes using active-vertex labels.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G=(V,E)\) have \(n=|V|\) vertices and \(m=|E|\) arcs, let \(A\subseteq V\setminus\{s,t\}\) be the active vertices, and define \(\Phi=\sum_{v\in A}h(v)\). For a nonsaturating push on an admissible residual arc \((u,v)\), the tail \(u\) becomes inactive. If \(v\) was inactive and becomes active, then admissibility gives \(h(u)=h(v)+1\), so the change in \(\Phi\) is \(-1\); if \(v\) was already active, the change is \(-h(u)\le -1\). Under the standard label bound, \(O(n^2)\) relabels, and \(O(nm)\) saturating pushes, the total positive variation of \(\Phi\) is \(O(n^2m)\). Consequently, the number of nonsaturating pushes is \(O(n^2m)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Using the sum of the labels of active intermediate vertices as a potential, every nonsaturating push decreases the potential by at least one. Standard bounds on label increases and saturating pushes limit the total positive variation to O(n²m), yielding O(n²m) nonsaturating pushes.
assumptions_latex: \(G=(V,E)\) is a finite network with \(n=|V|\) and \(m=|E|\).
Pushes and relabels obey the standard push-relabel rules and label bound.
There are \(O(n^2)\) relabel operations and \(O(nm)\) saturating pushes.

knowledge_statements.title: Pseudoflow State Space
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Capacity-feasible arc assignments without intermediate flow conservation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a directed network \(G=(V,E)\) with capacities \(c:E\to\mathbb{R}_{\ge0}\), a pseudoflow is a vector \(f\in\mathbb{R}^{E}\) satisfying \(0\le f(a)\le c(a)\) for every \(a\in E\), without requiring conservation at intermediate vertices. Its imbalance is \(b_f(v)=\sum_{(u,v)\in E}f(u,v)-\sum_{(v,w)\in E}f(v,w)\). A vertex is a surplus vertex when \(b_f(v)>0\), a deficit vertex when \(b_f(v)<0\), and balanced when \(b_f(v)=0\). Thus the state space consists of a capacity-feasible pseudoflow together with its induced residual network and imbalance vector.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A pseudoflow respects arc capacities but may violate conservation; its state records residual capacities and each vertex's surplus or deficit.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathcal P=\{f\in\mathbb R^E:0\le f(a)\le c(a)\ \forall a\in E\}\), with imbalance \(b_f\) as displayed.

knowledge_statements.title: Normalized-Tree Representation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Forest representation used by the Hochbaum pseudoflow algorithm.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A normalized-tree state represents a pseudoflow \(f\) by a spanning forest \(F\) whose components are rooted and whose tree arcs have positive residual capacity in the direction used by the component operations. Every nonroot vertex has exactly one parent arc. All flow imbalance is concentrated at component roots: \(b_f(v)=0\) for each nonroot \(v\). Contracting every tree component therefore yields a pseudoflow state in which merger, split, and root-transfer operations can be performed on components while preserving arc-capacity feasibility. Expanding the components recovers the original arc pseudoflow and its vertex imbalances.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A normalized forest gives each nonroot one parent and concentrates imbalance at roots, allowing pseudoflow updates to act on whole components.
assumptions_latex: \(F\) is a rooted spanning forest compatible with residual component operations.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: v\notin R(F)\Rightarrow b_f(v)=0,\quad\text{and contracting }F\text{ preserves the root imbalances}.
review_flags: exact Hochbaum normalized-tree invariants require an algorithm-specific source
tree-arc orientation and residual convention are source-dependent

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The exact normalized-tree conditions—including tree-arc orientation, residual status, and whether every nonroot must be balanced—are algorithm-specific and unsupported by a citation.

children.title: Rooted Component Structure
children.top_down_role: Component organization induced by the normalized-tree representation.

knowledge_statements.title: Rooted Component Structure
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Structural invariant of components in a normalized pseudoflow forest.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(F\) be a normalized rooted forest representing a capacity-feasible pseudoflow \(f\). Each weak component \(C\) of \(F\) has a unique root \(r_C\); every vertex of \(C\setminus\{r_C\}\) has one parent and zero imbalance. Consequently, \(\sum_{v\in C}b_f(v)=b_f(r_C)\). The component is surplus, balanced, or deficit according as this root imbalance is positive, zero, or negative. Component merger joins roots through an eligible residual arc, whereas splitting a parent arc produces two rooted components and transfers the corresponding aggregate imbalance to their roots.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Each forest component has one root, all nonroots are balanced, and the root carries the component's total surplus or deficit.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\sum_{v\in C}b_f(v)=b_f(r_C)\) for every component \(C\) of \(F\).
review_flags: algorithm-specific rooted-component invariant lacks a supplied source
merger and split conventions require source confirmation

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The aggregate-imbalance identity follows if all nonroots are balanced, but that invariant and the stated merger, split, and imbalance-transfer behavior require an algorithm-specific source.

knowledge_statements.title: Maximum Blocking-Cut Interface
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Cut certificate returned by a terminated pseudoflow phase.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f\) be the terminal pseudoflow state and let \(S\subseteq V\) contain \(s\) but not \(t\). If every arc from \(S\) to \(V\setminus S\) is saturated, every arc from \(V\setminus S\) to \(S\) carries zero flow, and the algorithm's terminal labels or component structure certify that no residual arc leaves \(S\), then \(S\) is a blocking cut. Its capacity \(c(\delta^+(S))\) is an upper bound on every feasible \(s\)-\(t\) flow value. If a recovered feasible flow has this value, the cut and flow jointly certify maximum flow and minimum cut.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A terminal pseudoflow exposes a cut with no outgoing residual arc; matching its capacity during flow recovery certifies optimality.
assumptions_latex: A feasible recovered flow has value \(c(\delta^+(S))\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: |f_{\mathrm{rec}}|=c(\delta^+(S))=\max\{|g|:g\text{ is a feasible }s\text{-}t\text{ flow}\}.

notation.meaning: source side of the blocking cut

review_flags: Hochbaum blocking-cut termination criterion lacks a supplied source
interface between terminal components and the cut requires source confirmation

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The generic flow-cut certificate is sound, but the leaf specifically concerns the Hochbaum terminal blocking-cut interface. No source establishes how terminal labels or components produce S or which termination conditions certify the cut.

knowledge_statements.title: Maximum-Flow Recovery
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Conversion of an optimal-cut pseudoflow into a feasible maximum flow.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given a capacity-feasible terminal pseudoflow \(f\) and its certified minimum cut \((S,V\setminus S)\), preserve all saturated forward cut arcs and zero reverse cut arcs. Within \(S\), route each positive imbalance back toward \(s\) through residual or represented-tree paths; within \(V\setminus S\), route flow from \(t\) or deficit roots to cancel negative imbalance. Each augmentation is limited by the available imbalance and path residual capacity, and saturated tree edges are split when necessary. Stop when every vertex other than \(s,t\) is balanced. The resulting feasible flow has value \(c(\delta^+(S))\) and is therefore maximum.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Cancel all nonterminal imbalances inside the two cut shores without changing saturated cut arcs; the resulting feasible flow matches the minimum-cut capacity.
assumptions_latex: The terminal pseudoflow is capacity feasible.
\((S,V\setminus S)\) is a certified minimum cut.
Recovery paths permit cancellation of all intermediate imbalances.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: b_{f'}(v)=0\ \forall v\notin\{s,t\},\qquad |f'|=c(\delta^+(S)).

notation.meaning: source side of the certified cut

review_flags: exact pseudoflow recovery procedure and path orientation require an algorithm-specific source
existence and complexity of recovery paths are not supported by supplied locators

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The existence and orientation of the proposed recovery paths, preservation of the cut arcs, and guaranteed cancellation of every intermediate imbalance are substantive algorithm-specific claims without source support.

knowledge_statements.title: Parametric Pseudoflow Variant
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Monotone parametric minimum-cut computation using warm-started pseudoflow states.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let capacities depend on a scalar \(\lambda\) over an ordered interval, with \(c_\lambda(s,v)\) nondecreasing, \(c_\lambda(v,t)\) nonincreasing, and all other capacities constant. Process breakpoints in increasing \(\lambda\), reusing the preceding normalized-tree pseudoflow and updating only arcs whose capacities change. Restore capacity feasibility, then apply pseudoflow merger, split, and relabel operations until a new blocking cut is obtained. With a consistent tie rule, choose minimum cuts \(S(\lambda)\) so that \(\lambda_1\le\lambda_2\) implies \(S(\lambda_1)\subseteq S(\lambda_2)\). Output the breakpoints and their nested source sets.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Warm-start pseudoflow across monotone capacity changes; consistent minimum cuts form nested source sets and change only at reported breakpoints.
assumptions_latex: All remaining capacities are independent of \(\lambda\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\lambda_1\le\lambda_2\Rightarrow S(\lambda_1)\subseteq S(\lambda_2)\) for a consistent extremal minimum-cut selection.

notation.meaning: selected source side of a minimum cut

breakpoint update and tie-breaking rules require source confirmation

children.title: Unit-Capacity Regime
children.top_down_role: Structural and complexity behavior when every relevant capacity is unit valued.

knowledge_statements.title: Unit-Capacity Regime
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Integral maximum flows in finite directed networks whose positive capacities are all one.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G=(V,E)\) be a finite directed graph with distinct vertices \(s,t\), let \(u:E\to\{0,1\}\), and define the positive-capacity support \(E_+=\{e\in E:u(e)=1\}\). There exists a maximum \(s\)-\(t\) flow \(f\) satisfying \(f(e)\in\{0,1\}\) for every \(e\in E\). A maximum flow may be chosen with no cyclic component, in which case it is the incidence sum of pairwise edge-disjoint directed \(s\)-\(t\) paths in \((V,E_+)\). Consequently, its value equals both the maximum number of pairwise edge-disjoint directed \(s\)-\(t\) paths in \((V,E_+)\) and the minimum cardinality of an \(s\)-\(t\) edge cut in \((V,E_+)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: With zero-one capacities, maximum flow equals both the largest number of edge-disjoint source–sink paths and the smallest source–sink edge cut in the subgraph of positive-capacity arcs.
assumptions_latex: \(G=(V,E)\) is finite and directed, with \(s\ne t\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\max |f|=\max\{\text{edge-disjoint }s\text{-}t\text{ paths in }(V,E_+)\}=\min\{|\delta^+(S)\cap E_+|:s\in S,\ t\notin S\}\).

notation.meaning: set of arcs having capacity one

children.title: Bounded-Integer Capacity Regime
children.top_down_role: Behavior for integer capacities restricted to a small magnitude range.

knowledge_statements.title: Bounded-Integer Capacity Regime
knowledge_statements.scope_note: The capacity bound is uniform over a family of finite networks.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A family of finite directed \(s\)-\(t\) networks is in the bounded-integer capacity regime if there is an integer constant \(B\ge 1\), independent of the instance size, such that every arc capacity satisfies \(u(e)\in\{0,1,\ldots,B\}\). For every instance in this regime, an integral maximum flow exists. Moreover, its value is bounded by \(|f|\le B\min\{\deg^+(s),\deg^-(t)\}\le B|E|\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Capacities are nonnegative integers bounded by a fixed instance-independent constant; maximum flows remain integral and have value at most the capacity incident to either terminal.
assumptions_latex: Each network is finite and directed.
The constant \(B\) does not grow with the instance.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(u(E)\subseteq\{0,\ldots,B\}\) and an integral maximum flow exists with \(|f|\le B|E|\).

children.title: Capacity-Magnitude Transition
children.top_down_role: Boundary between small-capacity advantages and general integer-capacity behavior.

knowledge_statements.title: Capacity-Magnitude Transition
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Magnitude dependence of the basic augmenting-path method for small integer capacities.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G=(V,E)\) have nonnegative integer capacities bounded by \(B\), and run the Ford–Fulkerson method from the zero flow, choosing any residual augmenting path each iteration. Every augmentation increases the flow value by at least one. Since every flow has value at most \(B|E|\), at most \(B|E|\) augmentations occur. If a residual path is found in \(O(|E|)\) time, the resulting bound is \(O(B|E|^2)\). Thus the bound is polynomial for fixed \(B\), but becomes pseudopolynomial when \(B\) is binary encoded and unbounded.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Basic augmenting paths take at most Bm augmentations and O(Bm²) time, polynomial for fixed B but pseudopolynomial when capacity magnitude is unbounded.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(N_{\mathrm{aug}}\le B|E|\) and \(T=O(B|E|^2)\).

knowledge_statements.title: Large Integer Capacities
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Binary-encoded integer capacities and the distinction between magnitude-dependent and scaling bounds.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a finite directed network with integer capacities and \(U=\max_{e\in E}u(e)\), arbitrary-path Ford–Fulkerson has the pseudopolynomial bound \(O(|E|^2U)\). A capacity-scaling implementation instead processes residual-capacity thresholds \(\Delta\) that are powers of two, beginning with the largest power satisfying \(\Delta\le U\). It performs \(O(|E|)\) augmentations per threshold and \(O(1+\log U)\) thresholds, giving \(O(|E|^2(1+\log U))\) time with linear-time path searches. This is polynomial in the binary capacity length.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Large binary capacities expose Ford–Fulkerson’s pseudopolynomial dependence on U; capacity scaling replaces U by logarithmically many magnitude phases.
assumptions_latex: Capacities are nonnegative integers encoded in binary.
Residual searches and updates take \(O(|E|)\) time.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(T_{\mathrm{FF}}=O(|E|^2U)\), whereas \(T_{\mathrm{scaling}}=O(|E|^2(1+\log U))\).

children.title: Rational-Capacity Regime

knowledge_statements.title: Rational-Capacity Regime
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact reduction of a finite rational-capacity instance to an integer-capacity instance.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let every capacity \(u(e)\) be a nonnegative rational number, and choose a positive integer \(D\) such that \(Du(e)\in\mathbb Z\) for all \(e\in E\). Define \(u'(e)=Du(e)\). Multiplication by \(D\) bijects feasible flows for \(u\) with feasible flows for \(u'\), preserves their ordering by value, and maps every cut capacity to \(D\) times its original capacity. Hence \(f\) is maximum for \(u\) exactly when \(Df\) is maximum for \(u'\), and the optimum values satisfy \(\nu(u')=D\nu(u)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A common denominator scales a rational-capacity maximum-flow instance exactly to an integer-capacity instance, scaling every flow and cut value by the same factor.
assumptions_latex: Every capacity is a nonnegative rational number.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f\in F(u)\Longleftrightarrow Df\in F(Du)\) and \(\nu(Du)=D\nu(u)\).

notation.meaning: set of feasible flows under capacities u

children.title: Arbitrary Real-Capacity Regime
children.top_down_role: Structural behavior with unrestricted real capacity data.

knowledge_statements.title: Arbitrary Real-Capacity Regime
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional max-flow/min-cut equality for nonnegative real capacities.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(G=(V,E)\) be a finite directed graph with distinct vertices \(s,t\), and let \(u:E\to\mathbb R_{\ge0}\). Then a maximum feasible \(s\)-\(t\) flow exists, a minimum-capacity \(s\)-\(t\) cut exists, and their values are equal:
\[\max_f |f|=\min_{S\subseteq V:\,s\in S,\,t\notin S}\sum_{e\in\delta^+(S)}u(e).\]
No rationality or integrality of \(u\) is required for this equality. However, the conclusion does not assert the existence of an integral or rational optimal flow when capacities are arbitrary real numbers.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: On every finite network, max-flow/min-cut equality holds for arbitrary nonnegative real capacities, although an integral or rational optimum need not exist.
assumptions_latex: \(G=(V,E)\) is finite and directed, with \(s\ne t\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\max_f|f|=\min_{S:\,s\in S,\,t\notin S}u(\delta^+(S))\).

notation.meaning: arcs directed from S to its complement
sum of capacities of arcs leaving S

children.title: Exact-Arithmetic Boundary
children.top_down_role: Limits imposed by representation and comparison of nonintegral capacities.

knowledge_statements.title: Exact-Arithmetic Boundary
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Boundary between rational Turing inputs and unspecified exact computation over arbitrary reals.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: In the standard Turing model, a capacity vector is an exact finite input when each capacity has a finite encoding, in particular when \(u(e)\in\mathbb Q_{\ge0}\) is given in binary. Arithmetic and comparison costs must then be measured in terms of total bit length. An unrestricted real capacity \(u(e)\in\mathbb R_{\ge0}\) need not have any finite exact encoding. Therefore a claimed exact running time for arbitrary real capacities is not a Turing-model complexity statement unless a representation and permitted exact operations are specified, such as an algebraic-number encoding or a real-RAM oracle model.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Rational capacities admit finite exact encodings; arbitrary reals do not automatically define Turing inputs, so exact complexity requires an explicit representation or real-arithmetic model.
assumptions_latex: Exact computation is interpreted in a specified computational model.
Input length means binary encoding length in the Turing model.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(u\in\mathbb Q_{\ge0}^{E}\) has a standard finite binary encoding, while \(u\in\mathbb R_{\ge0}^{E}\) requires an additional representation assumption.

children.title: Sparse-Network Regime

knowledge_statements.title: Sparse-Network Regime
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Asymptotic sparsity for a family of directed maximum-flow instances.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a family of finite directed networks \(G_n=(V_n,E_n)\), write \(n=|V_n|\) and \(m=|E_n|\). The family is in the sparse-network regime when there is a constant \(C\) independent of \(n\) such that \(m\le Cn\) for every sufficiently large instance. Equivalently, \(m=O(n)\). In this regime the average outdegree \(m/n\) is bounded, and any storage representation using \(O(n+m)\) words occupies \(O(n)\) words.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A network family is sparse when its number of arcs grows only linearly with its number of vertices; adjacency-list storage is then linear.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(m=O(n)\), hence \(m/n=O(1)\) and \(O(n+m)=O(n)\).

knowledge_statements.title: Dense-Network Regime
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Asymptotically maximal arc density for simple directed network families.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a family of finite simple directed networks \(G_n=(V_n,E_n)\) without parallel arcs, write \(n=|V_n|\) and \(m=|E_n|\). The family is in the dense-network regime when constants \(c>0\) and \(n_0\) exist such that \(m\ge cn^2\) whenever \(n\ge n_0\). Since \(m\le n(n-1)\), this is equivalent to \(m=\Theta(n^2)\). Adjacency-matrix storage uses \(\Theta(n^2)\) entries, matching the order of the arc count.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A simple directed network family is dense when it contains quadratically many arcs, the maximum possible asymptotic order.
assumptions_latex: Networks are simple and directed, without parallel arcs.

children.title: Density-Sensitive Complexity

knowledge_statements.title: Density-Sensitive Complexity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Edmonds–Karp complexity specialized by network density.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: On a finite directed network with \(n=|V|\) vertices and \(m=|E|\) arcs, the Edmonds–Karp shortest-augmenting-path algorithm performs \(O(nm)\) augmentations. Breadth-first search and augmentation take \(O(m)\) time per iteration, so the total running time is \(O(nm^2)\), independent of capacity magnitudes. Substitution yields \(O(n^3)\) time when \(m=O(n)\) and \(O(n^5)\) time when \(m=\Theta(n^2)\). Thus an \((n,m)\)-parameterized bound distinguishes sparse and dense regimes even when the same algorithm is used.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Edmonds–Karp runs in O(nm²): O(n³) on sparse networks and O(n⁵) on dense simple networks.
assumptions_latex: Sparse means \(m=O(n)\), while dense simple means \(m=\Theta(n^2)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(T(n,m)=O(nm^2)\), giving \(O(n^3)\) for sparse and \(O(n^5)\) for dense networks.

knowledge_statements.title: Acyclic Networks
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Flow decomposition specialized to directed acyclic networks.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G=(V,E)\) be a finite directed acyclic graph with source \(s\), sink \(t\), and a feasible nonnegative \(s\)-\(t\) flow \(f\). Because \(G\) contains no directed cycle, the flow-decomposition theorem has no cyclic component: there exist directed \(s\)-\(t\) paths \(P_1,\ldots,P_k\) and coefficients \(\lambda_i>0\) such that \(f=\sum_{i=1}^k\lambda_i\chi^{P_i}\), with \(k\le |E|\). Consequently, every feasible flow is completely represented by weighted source–sink paths, and topological order is respected by every such path.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every feasible flow on a directed acyclic network decomposes solely into at most m weighted source–sink paths, with no cyclic-flow component.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f=\sum_{i=1}^{k}\lambda_i\chi^{P_i}\) for directed \(s\)-\(t\) paths, where \(k\le |E|\).
